274.title: Yajnavalkya's two words
274.hook: a king offers a thousand cows to the wisest sage, and the winner gives the self no label
274.carry: neti neti: you are the one who sees
274.howItsDone: In Vedanta, jnana yoga is practiced by studying the Upanishads with a teacher, reflecting on them, and meditating on the self as the witness of body and mind; 'not this, not this' (neti neti) is one of its classic tools.

segments.voice: Last week: bhakti yoga, and the line dasya and vatsalya: God as king, God as child. Nine doors, the Tamil saints, Mira, Tulsidas, Surdas, and a street full of kirtan. Today, the third path.
screen: `DASYA AND VATSALYA: GOD AS KING, GOD AS CHILD.`

segments.voice: King Janaka wants to know who is the wisest sage in the land. So he pens up a thousand cows and ties gold to their horns. The wisest of you, he tells the gathered sages, may drive them home. Nobody moves. Then Yajnavalkya calls to his student: drive them home. The hall erupts. You think you're the wisest? Yajnavalkya shrugs. I bow to the wisest. I just want the cows. So, one by one, the sages line up to test him. The last one keeps pushing: then describe the self. The real I. And Yajnavalkya answers with two words.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `I JUST WANT THE COWS.` → `DESCRIBE THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Neti, neti. Not this, not this. The story is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the oldest, and those two words are a classic doorway into the third path of yoga: jnana. Jnana comes from the Sanskrit root jna, to know, a cousin of the English word know and the Greek gnosis. But jnana doesn't mean information. You can't look it up. It means knowing the way you know you're awake: direct, from the inside. Karma yoga asked what you do. Bhakti asked who you love. Jnana asks who is doing and loving in the first place. So why won't Yajnavalkya give the self a label? Because whatever you can point at is not it. Not the body. Not the breath. Not the thoughts, not the feelings. Anything you can observe is something you're observing, so it can't be the observer. Elsewhere in the same Upanishad he asks: by what would one know the knower? Your eye can see everything except itself. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, especially in Vedanta: the atman, your real self, isn't the body or the mind but the awareness that knows them. So the jnana path works by subtraction, not addition. And here's where it meets your life. Someone at a party asks, so, what do you do? You give a job, a city, a school, a family. Every one is true, and every one can be pointed at. Neti, neti: not wrong, just not the whole of you. This week: a riverbank, a wife who turns down a fortune, and a boy bent in eight places.
screen: `NETI, NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `JNA: TO KNOW, FROM THE INSIDE.` · `WHO KNOWS THE KNOWER?` · `ATMAN: THE ONE WHO SEES.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THE ONE WHO SEES.`

segments.voice: Notice the weight of your body on the seat and say inwardly, not this; then the breath, not this; then a thought passing through, not this, either. Don't push anything away; just notice it's being noticed, and rest as the one noticing, without trying to describe it. If it slips away, begin again.
Jnana yoga. The path of knowledge: not information, but knowing from the inside who you are. Its first tool is neti, neti, not this, not this.
Your line: neti neti, you are the one who sees. Every label you can point at is not quite it. Day two seventy-four.

275.title: The tenth man
275.hook: ten travelers cross a river, count themselves, and find only nine
275.carry: you are the tenth: the self was never missing
275.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers often use the parable of the tenth man to show that self-knowledge isn't gaining something new but recognizing what was always present; students then practice discerning the witness from what it witnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana yoga, and Yajnavalkya's two words, neti, neti. Not this, not this. Today, a story Vedanta teachers tell.

Ten friends set out on a trip together, and they have to ford a fast river. They wade across, holding on to each other, and scramble up the far bank, soaked. The leader, to be safe, counts heads. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Nine. He counts again. Nine. Someone's been swept away. Each of the others counts, and each gets nine too. They sit down on the riverbank and weep for their lost friend.
screen: `TEN FRIENDS CROSS A RIVER.` → `ONE, TWO… NINE.` → `THEY WEEP FOR THE LOST ONE.`

segments.voice: A traveler walking by asks what's wrong. They tell him: there were ten of us, and one has drowned. He looks at them, and counts. Ten. He asks the leader to count again. Nine. Then the traveler touches the leader on the shoulder and says: you are the tenth. That's the whole story. It's told in Advaita Vedanta texts because it shows how neti neti works in practice. The leader wasn't missing. He was doing the counting, so he never counted himself. He was looking everywhere but at the looker. And notice: nothing new was found. No one came out of the river. The grief ended the moment he recognized what had been there the whole time. That's why jnana is called knowledge, not achievement. Hindu teachers say the atman, your real self, is never lost and never gained. You don't become the self. You stop leaving it out of the count. So how do you practice it? Neti neti in real life is a kind of honest sorting. When you feel, I am angry, look closer: anger is showing up, and something is aware of it. Not this. When you think, I am a failure, look closer: a thought is showing up. Not this. You don't deny the anger or the thought. You just stop counting them as the counter. What's left is the one who was looking. The Upanishads have a phrase for this recognition, and later teachers repeat it again and again: you are that.
screen: `THE TRAVELER COUNTS: TEN.` · `YOU ARE THE TENTH.` · `NOTHING NEW WAS FOUND.` · `STOP LEAVING YOURSELF OUT.` · then, large: `THE SELF WAS NEVER MISSING.`

segments.voice: Count, like the leader on the riverbank: one, the body sitting; two, the breath; three, a sound in the room; four, a thought; five, whatever mood is here. Then pause and ask: who's counting? Don't answer with a word; just turn toward the counter, the way the traveler turned the leader around, and when counting starts again, let it.
Jnana yoga, in practice. Neti neti sets aside what can be counted, the body, the thoughts, the moods, and turns you toward the counter. You are the tenth.
Your line: you are the tenth. The self was never missing; it was doing the counting. Day two seventy-five, counted.

276.title: Maitreyi's question
276.hook: a husband offers to split the property; his wife asks for something else
276.carry: hear it, question it, live in it
276.tomorrow: The man on the lane in Kashi
276.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students traditionally study the Upanishads and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher (shravana), work through doubts and questions (manana), and then practice sustained contemplation (nididhyasana).

segments.voice: Yesterday: ten friends, a river, and the leader who forgot to count himself. You are the tenth. Today, a question worth more than a fortune.

The sage Yajnavalkya, the one who said neti neti, decides to leave home and live as a wandering monk. He has two wives, and he calls one of them, Maitreyi, to settle things. Let me divide what I have between you and Katyayani, he says. It's a fair, sensible offer. Maitreyi asks one question. If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich. That's all. And she says: then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know instead.
screen: `LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.` → `WOULD IT MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya is delighted, and he teaches her. In that conversation in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, he gives a line that became the backbone of the jnana path. Paraphrased: the self is what should be seen. It should be heard about, reflected on, and deeply meditated on. Much later, the teacher Shankara and those who followed him made those verbs a method, three steps still taught in Vedanta schools, and the reason Hindu teachers often welcome a student's questions. First, shravana: hearing. You listen to the teaching, from the Upanishads and from a teacher, carefully, the way Maitreyi listened. Not skimming. Hearing. Second, manana: reflecting. You argue with what you've heard and raise every doubt. Does this make sense? What about this objection? Shankara didn't want blind belief; he spent pages answering objections. Third, nididhyasana: deep, sustained meditation. Once the doubts have settled, you dwell on the teaching until it's no longer an idea you hold but the way you see. Hear it, test it, soak in it. Shankara also insisted on a teacher. Not a guru to worship blindly, but someone who has walked the road and can point, like the traveler who turned the leader around. And notice where this began. Not with a debate. With a woman who turned down her share of a fortune and asked for the truth.
screen: `MAITREYI TURNS DOWN THE FORTUNE.` · `SHRAVANA: HEARING.` · `MANANA: QUESTIONING.` · `NIDIDHYASANA: LIVING IN IT.` · then, large: `HEAR IT, QUESTION IT, LIVE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Take one small line, I am aware, and first just hear it, letting the words land. Then reflect: is it true right now, is there awareness here? Raise any doubt you honestly have. If it holds, soak in it: don't repeat the words, just rest in what they point to, the plain fact of being aware.
Jnana yoga, Shankara's method: shravana, manana, nididhyasana. Hearing the teaching, reflecting on it, and meditating on it until it becomes how you see.
Your line: hear it, question it, live in it. On this road, even your doubts get a step of their own. See you next time.

277.title: The man on the lane in Kashi
277.hook: on a narrow lane in Kashi, the great teacher tells a man to step aside, and the man asks who should move
277.carry: the same self lives in everyone
277.tomorrow: The boy bent in eight places
277.howItsDone: Advaita teachers say the one self (atman) is the same in every being, and tell the Kashi story of Shankara to show it; students also work on four qualifications (sadhana chatushtaya): discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues of a steady mind, and longing for freedom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maitreyi, who turned down a fortune, and Shankara's three steps of jnana yoga. Your line: hear it, question it, live in it. Today, a teacher stopped on a narrow lane.

There's a story told about Shankara in Varanasi, the holy city also called Kashi. He's walking to the river with his students, and on a narrow lane a man comes toward them with his dogs, a man from a community that the purity rules of the day kept at a distance. Shankara says what the custom said to say: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks: which should move away from which? This body from that body? Both are made of food. Or this self from that self? There's only one. Shankara, the story says, stopped, and bowed to him.
screen: `A NARROW LANE IN KASHI.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `WHICH SHOULD MOVE FROM WHICH?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Shankara then composed five verses, the Manisha Panchakam, each ending, roughly: whoever sees this way is my teacher, whatever his birth. Here's the teaching under the story. If your real self, the atman, isn't the body, then it's the same awareness in everyone: the monk, the man with the dogs, and you. The Gita says it too: the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and the one who eats dogs. Hindu society did draw hard lines of caste and purity, and that history is real. Many Hindus today point to this story when they say those lines never reach the self. Shankara taught the one self for years, and it took a stranger to make him live it. Knowing isn't living. So texts in his tradition, like the Vivekachudamani, list four qualities a student needs. Viveka: telling the lasting from the passing. Vairagya: loosening your grip on what passes. A steady mind: calm, patience, trust, focus. And “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free. Viveka caught up with Shankara on the lane: the rule was about bodies, and the self is not a body. And today? Think of the person you're quick to rank below you: the new kid, the cleaner, the one with the accent. The same self is looking out of their eyes.
screen: `WHOEVER SEES THIS WAY IS MY TEACHER.` · `ONE SELF IN EVERYONE.` · `VIVEKA: LASTING FROM PASSING.` · `KNOWING ISN'T LIVING.` · then, large: `THE SAME SELF LIVES IN EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Sort things gently as they arise: a sound, passing; a twinge in the knee, passing; a worry about tomorrow, a pleasant memory, passing too. Don't push any of it away; then notice what hasn't passed through all of it, the noticing, and rest there for a few breaths. If you want, remember the man on the lane, and let there be no one to step aside from.

Jnana yoga, on the lane in Kashi: the same self in everyone. Its students need four qualities: viveka, telling lasting from passing; vairagya, dispassion; a steady mind; and “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free.
Your line: the same self lives in everyone. On a lane in Kashi, it came back as a question: which should move from which? Two seventy-seven, done.

278.title: The boy bent in eight places
278.hook: a boy bent in eight places walks into a king's court, and the court laughs
278.carry: the self is not the skin
278.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and chanted in many Advaita circles as a direct statement of non-dual teaching, often studied alongside the Upanishads; its opening questions from King Janaka frame the whole text.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lane in Kashi, and the four qualifications. Discernment, dispassion, a steady mind, longing to be free. Your line: the same self lives in everyone.

An unborn child corrects his own father. The Mahabharata tells of a scholar named Kahoda who recited the Vedas while his wife was pregnant, and from inside the womb the child pointed out his mistakes. The father, stung, cursed him: you'll be born bent in eight places. Then Kahoda went to the court of King Janaka, lost a debate to the court's champion, and never came home. The boy was born bent, just as the curse said. They called him Ashtavakra: eight bends. At twelve he learned what had happened, and set out, crooked and limping, for that court to win his father back.
screen: `CORRECTED FROM THE WOMB.` → `ASHTAVAKRA: EIGHT BENDS.` → `A BOY GOES TO THE KING'S COURT.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata's telling, the boy talks his way past the gatekeeper, defeats the court's champion debater, and his father is restored. People love to tell a popular addition: when Ashtavakra walked in, the courtiers laughed at his body, and he laughed back. Why are you laughing? they asked. I thought this was an assembly of the wise, he said. It's a gathering of leather-workers. You only judge the skin. Whether that exchange is old or newer, it's the jnana teaching in one joke: the atman, the real self, is not the body. A twelve-year-old in a crooked body had out-argued the champion. It fits the book that carries his name. The Ashtavakra Gita is a short Sanskrit dialogue between the sage and King Janaka. Nobody knows when it was written, or by whom. It opens with the king asking three questions. Paraphrased: how is knowledge gained? How will freedom come? How is detachment reached? Tell me this, my lord. How do I know. How am I free. How do I let go. And notice who's asking: a king, with everything. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names Janaka as one who reached perfection through action, a king who lived in the world and wasn't owned by it. The answer he gets, tomorrow, doesn't ask him to give up his throne. And today? We still size each other up by skin: height, color, a limp, a wheelchair, a bad photo.

279.title: Ashtavakra's answer
279.hook: a king asks how to be free, and the sage says: right now
279.carry: you are the witness, free right now
279.tomorrow: The tiger who thought he was a goat
279.howItsDone: Students of the Ashtavakra Gita often chant or read its first chapter slowly, pausing on each verse, and use its list of the five elements as a contemplation: noticing each as known, and resting as the knower.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra, the sage of eight bends, and King Janaka's three questions. How do I know? How am I free? How do I let go? Your line: the self is not the skin. Today, the answer.

Back in King Janaka's palace. The king who has everything sits before a young sage bent in eight places and asks: how do I know, how am I free, how do I let go? In the old stories, a seeker who asks that gets a long program. Twelve years in a forest. A thousand rules. A ladder with a hundred rungs. Ashtavakra starts gently. Then, a few verses in, he says something so bold you may read it twice.
screen: `BACK IN JANAKA'S PALACE.` → `HOW AM I FREE?` → `THEN THE ANSWER GETS BOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening of the reply, paraphrased. If you want freedom, my child, treat the pull of the senses like poison, and drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth like nectar. The next verse turns everything. You are not earth. You are not water, or fire, or air, or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these: awareness itself. The five elements that make up everything, and you're none of them. You're the one they appear to. Then the verse that stops people. If you set the body aside and rest in awareness, then right now, this very moment, you'll be happy, at peace, and free. Not after twelve years. Now. A little later he adds: right and wrong, pleasure and pain, belong to the mind, not to you. You're not the doer, not the one who enjoys the results. You were always free. This is the Hindu teaching of the sakshi, the witness: the self watches body and mind and is never caught by them. Is that too easy? Teachers say it's simple, not easy. Nothing has to be built. But everything you keep counting as yourself has to be seen through, the way the leader by the river had to stop counting and turn around. The Ashtavakra Gita doesn't give you a ladder. It points at the floor you're already standing on. So the night before a big test, the panic is real, and it's seen. You are the one seeing it.
screen: `SENSES AS POISON, VIRTUES AS NECTAR.` · `YOU ARE NOT EARTH, WATER, FIRE.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.` · `RIGHT NOW: HAPPY, AT PEACE, FREE.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THE WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Walk Ashtavakra's list slowly: earth, the weight of the body on the seat; water, the moisture in the mouth; fire, the warmth of the skin; air, the breath; space, the room around you, each one noticed, none of them what you are. Then, for a few breaths, rest as the one noticing, right now. If the mind says it's not working, that's a thought too: noticed.
Jnana yoga, in the Ashtavakra Gita's answer: you are not the elements, but the witness of them, awareness itself; rest there, and you're free now.
Your line: you are the witness, free right now. Not earth, not water, not fire: the one they appear to. That's day two seventy-nine.

280.title: The tiger who thought he was a goat
280.hook: a tiger cub raised by goats eats grass and bleats, until another tiger shows him the water
280.carry: know yourself free, and you are free
280.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers present karma, bhakti and jnana (often with raja yoga, meditation) as paths suited to different temperaments, while also teaching that they support one another; parables like Ramakrishna's tiger raised among goats are used to show that the self is already free and only has to be recognized.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra's bold answer. You are the witness, free right now. Today, the last day of jnana, and of the three paths.

Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, told this one. A tigress leaps on a flock of goats, gives birth as she springs, and dies. Her cub grows up among the goats. It eats grass. It bleats. When danger comes, it runs with the herd. Years later, a wild tiger attacks the same flock and stops, astonished. A tiger, eating grass? It drags the young one to a pond. Look at your face in the water. It's just like mine. It gives him a taste of meat. And slowly, the tiger who thought he was a goat lets out a roar.
screen: `A TIGER RAISED BY GOATS.` → `A TIGER, EATING GRASS?` → `LOOK IN THE WATER. THE ROAR.`

segments.voice: The young tiger was never a goat. He was bound by what he took himself to be. In Ramakrishna's telling, the wild tiger is like the teacher, holding up the water. The Ashtavakra Gita says it in its first chapter. Paraphrased: whoever takes themselves to be free is free, and whoever takes themselves to be bound is bound. And it adds: the popular saying is true, as you think, so you become. Ya matih sa gatih. This isn't positive thinking. It's about identity, the heart of jnana. In Vedanta's reading, the atman, your real self, is already free, and bondage is mistaking yourself for the body, the job, the moods. Lose a job, and you can feel finished, because you took yourself to be the job. Jnana would say: that's the goat talking. Look in the water. That's the end of our jnana week: neti neti, the tenth man, Maitreyi, the lane in Kashi, Ashtavakra, and today the tiger at the pond. It's also the end of three weeks on the three paths. Karma: offer the work. Bhakti: love as the road. Jnana: know who you are. Some teachers see separate roads for the doer, the lover, the thinker. Vivekananda did, and added a fourth, raja yoga, the path of meditation. Others point to the Gita, which weaves all three through its chapters. Next: the school that says not two.
screen: `HE WAS NEVER A GOAT.` · `FREE IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.` · `THAT'S THE GOAT TALKING.` · `KARMA. BHAKTI. JNANA.` · then, large: `KNOW YOURSELF FREE.`

segments.voice: Try the three paths in one sitting: for karma, think of one piece of work waiting for you, and offer it; for bhakti, bring to mind someone or something you love, and let that love be there. Then, for jnana, ask quietly who is offering, who is loving, and don't answer; just rest as the one who's asking. If a sense of freedom comes, let it; if it doesn't, that's fine too.
Jnana yoga, the path of knowledge: knowing yourself as the free witness. Today's verse: whoever takes themselves as free is free. As you think, so you become.
Your line: know yourself free, and you are free. The tiger was a tiger all along. And that's the three paths, walked.
